title: PI3Kδ is selectively inhibited by roginolisib by stabilizing the C-terminal helix kα12
abstract: Phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) are major regulators of cell growth, proliferation and signalling, constituting key therapeutic targets in cancer, inflammation, and other diseases. Individual class I PI3K isoforms control key cellular functions, imposing the need to generate isoform-specific inhibition for therapeutic intervention. Roginolisib is a selective PI3Kδ inhibitor that shows promise for the treatment of cancer. Using a combination of X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics simulations, and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, we describe the mechanism driving roginolisib's potent and isoform-selective inhibition of PI3Kδ. Roginolisib uniquely stabilises the catalytic C-terminal helix kα12, locking the enzyme in an inactive conformation. This binding mode also results in more sustained inhibition of phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate formation in tumour samples of CLL patients. Inhibition of PI3Ks by stabilization of helix kα12 into an inactive conformation has not, to the best of our knowledge, been described before and may provide the basis for novel, more selective and effective pharmacological strategies.

title: Prior preferences interfere with the associative learning of food values
abstract: Addressing unhealthy behaviors requires learning and implementing healthier options. Ecologically, we rarely undergo associative learning in naive environments; our prior preferences confound the learning process. This is perhaps especially true for food, for which we have strong, diverse preferences that may undermine the associative learning policies central to dietary interventions. This preregistered study investigates the flexibility of updating food values using a probabilistic reversal learning task where participants predicted outcomes associated with food stimuli varying in personal preference. The task alternated between "Congruent" blocks, reinforcing pre-existing associations, and "Incongruent" blocks, reversing them. Across independent cohorts (n = 279), we found that starting condition had a surprising, lasting effect on food-value association updating, with initial reinforcement of food-value priors potentiating learning inflexibility. Rigidity was further evident for liked food items, whereas disliked foods were adaptable to changing value associations. Additionally, associations with positive outcomes were learned more readily than negative ones, suggesting positive reinforcement may be more effective in informing food-based learning. These findings highlight the importance of reinforcement in shaping food-value associations and underscore its relevance to promoting healthier eating habits.

title: Preserved higher-order mentalising during strategic interactions after medial prefrontal cortex damage
abstract: Abstract Mentalising, the ability to infer the beliefs and intentions of others, is essential for successful social interaction. Previous studies have implicated the medial prefrontal cortex in mentalising, but whether this region is necessary for higher-order mentalising remains unclear. Here we show that people with focal damage to the medial prefrontal cortex retain the ability to engage in higher-order mentalising during a strategic social game. We compare their performance with patients with brain damage in other regions and lesion-free participants. Individuals with medial prefrontal cortex damage achieve similar rewards and use comparable mentalising strategies, but they are slower when making strategic decisions. Computational modelling indicates that this slowing reflects a greater tendency to require evidence before committing to a choice. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping identifies medial prefrontal regions linked to altered decision processes rather than mentalising. These findings suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex supports strategic decisions while higher-order mentalising remains intact.

title: Giant step-boundary-triggered nonlocal modulation of magnetization reversal in multi-stepped van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3GaTe2
How does hard magnetic soft matter deform?
abstract: Abstract Hard Magnetic Soft Materials, i.e., elastomers seeded with hard magnetic particles, convert magnetic energy into complex motion and have become central to the design of untethered soft robots, biomedical devices, and, in general, for enabling fast, wireless actuation. Their behavior depends critically on how the surrounding soft matrix deforms and transmits torque to each magnetized inclusion, yet there is no consensus on the correct mapping between macroscopic strain and microscopic motion. Competing models predict conflicting particle rotations and magnetic responses under identical loads. Here, we construct counterexamples that show the key shortcomings in these models, and then establish a first-principles framework that leads to an optimal deformation mapping. The resulting closed-form law unifies conflicting models and shows that they are, in fact, simply different limits of our general approach. Our work permits the rational design of magnetically actuated soft devices and a unified view of deformation in magnetic soft matter, and broadly, in similar architectured materials.

title: Fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography using explicit neural fields
abstract: Abstract Multimodal fluorescence and phase imaging provides complementary information about biological samples. However, existing simultaneous fluorescence-phase techniques primarily operate in transmission mode and are limited to thin specimens, restricting their use in thick tissues and in vivo applications. Although multiphoton microscopy enables deep-tissue fluorescence imaging, combining it with three-dimensional refractive-index (RI) imaging remains challenging because few methods can reconstruct the RI of bulky, label-free tissues in reflection mode at subcellular resolution. Here, we introduce fluorescence-illuminated diffraction tomography (FDT), which reconstructs the 3D RI of label-free and fluorescence-labeled objects from diffracted fluorescence images acquired in reflection mode under two-photon excitation. FDT uses the transport of intensity equation and a self-supervised neural network based on explicit neural fields. Compared with state-of-the-art implicit neural fields, this approach improves computational speed, reconstruction accuracy, and interpretability. We demonstrate FDT in two experimental regimes: reconstructing the 3D RI of label-free tissues up to 300 μ m thick placed on a fluorescent substrate, and reconstructing the 3D RI of fluorescence-labeled, 3D-cultured cells without transmission-side access using fluorescence emitted by the cells themselves. FDT establishes a foundation for accessible reflection-mode multimodal fluorescence-phase imaging in complex biological systems.

title: Large-scale identical-location electron microscopy enables quantifying nanoparticulate electrocatalyst degradation
abstract: Abstract Fuel cells convert chemical energy into electricity, and their performance relies on electrocatalysts whose durability during operation remains poorly understood. Deep mechanistic insight into electrocatalyst stability is essential to design durable, resource-efficient fuel cells. Nanoparticulate electrocatalysts degrade via diverse nanoscale processes, yet particle-to-particle heterogeneity in structure, support interaction, and local microenvironment make true particle-level quantification and understanding impossible with classical approaches. Here we scale up identical-location scanning transmission electron microscopy, which repeatedly images the very same nanoparticles, to track the structural evolution of hundreds of carbon-supported platinum-cobalt nanoparticles, a prototypical oxygen reduction reaction electrocatalyst. We present a three-step image analysis workflow comprising segmentation, tracking, and degradation-event classification with progressive automation, including machine-learning-assisted detection of overlapping particles. By pairing nanoscale resolution and local history with population-level statistics, the pipeline enables unbiased identification and quantification of degradation pathways across statistically meaningful particle sets. We reveal particle size- and shape-dependent effects, showing that smaller and irregular nanoparticles are more prone to detachment, and provide a data-driven framework for probing electrocatalyst degradation at scale.

title: Programable extracellular matrix heterogeneity directs least-resistance migration in three dimensions
abstract: Abstract Cell migration through three-dimensional (3D) extracellular matrices (ECMs) is central to development, immune response, and cancer metastasis, yet how cells navigate mechanically heterogeneous environments remains poorly understood. Here we introduce a light-guided in situ ECM photopatterning method that enables micron-scale, programmable modulation of matrix mechanics within 3D collagen networks. Using this platform, we engineer well-defined mechanical barriers around tumor spheroids. Both bulk rheology and micromechanical measurements show photocrosslinking increases local stiffness by up to fivefold, creating sharp mechanical gradients. Strikingly, even small localized barriers strongly suppress cell dissemination over extended spatial ranges, far exceeding their geometric footprint. Systematic variation of barrier geometry reveals that invasion is not governed by direct steric obstruction but by long-range mechanical modulation of the ECM, which reshapes least-resistance migration paths and is tightly coupled to transitions in migratory phenotype. These results establish a quantitative framework for how microscale mechanical heterogeneity directs collective invasion and suggest that cancer cells integrate nonlocal mechanical cues to modulate their phenotype transitions when navigating complex environments.

title: A dual-attribution framework reveals how foreign investment and trade redistribute cobalt availability
Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda)
abstract: Abstract The diversification of herbivorous dinosaurs and the rise of angiosperms in the Late Cretaceous are each well established, but the link between them is debated. Broad-scale diversity patterns in the two groups appear not to closely align, and there is no direct evidence of dinosaur adaptation to angiosperm-based diets. Here we describe Infernogallus jamesi gen. et. sp. nov., a diminutive caenagnathid oviraptorosaur, and show that these theropods were specialised herbivores that originated alongside the rise of fleshy angiosperm fruits. The nearly complete, articulated skull of Infernogallus jamesi —the first for the clade—reveals drastic changes to the adductor musculature organisation, unique in non-avian theropods but converged upon by extant frugivorous parrots. These modifications enabled extensive oral processing of soft food using anteroposterior movement of the mandible and occlusion of ridges and grooves on opposed elements. Altogether, this attests to a highly specialised herbivorous diet in caenagnathids, which likely consisted in large part of fleshy angiosperm fruits, which increased in size and diversity in concert with the radiation of oviraptorosaurs. Caenagnathids thus provide one of the strongest candidates for angiosperm-based diet adaptations in dinosaurs, but their role in the Late Cretaceous proliferation of fruit—which shaped early Cenozoic flora—remains unclear.

title: A self-limiting mechanotransduction feedback loop ensures robust organ formation
Beyond site-specific archaeological prospection: Spectral-geometry reveals cross-site cropmark signals in satellite data
abstract: Abstract Remote sensing has long supported archaeological prospection, mainly through the detection of cropmarks, a key archaeological proxy expressed as spectral vegetation anomalies over subsurface features. Yet, cropmark detection is still assumed in the literature to be highly site-specific, governed by local agronomic and environmental conditions. Using multispectral Sentinel-2 data from three European archaeological sites, we show that models trained in one landscape can recover meaningful archaeological proxy signals in other locations. By relying strictly on satellite spectral signatures for training, our models achieve measurable cross-location transferability without incorporating ancillary environmental data. We find that cross-site performance arises not from geographic proximity but from the spectral-geometric similarity of vegetation responses, and that transferability is strongly directional. We quantify this relationship through a Directional Strength Score (DSS), derived from monthly subcluster distances under multiple norms, which captures directional geometric similarity and correlates strongly with machine-learning performance. To keep the analysis grounded in the underlying spectral signal, we relied on architecturally restrained nonlinear classifiers (SVM and constrained XGBoost) and used NDVI-identified phenophases to align training and evaluation with comparable seasonal windows. Taken together, these results demonstrate that partial, spectrally mediated cross-location cropmark detection is feasible and that the underlying vegetation responses exhibit stable spectral structure, with spectral geometry offering a clear interpretive lens on why these signals can transfer across sites. Leveraging globally harmonized satellite data, this approach offers a scalable complement to uneven historical aerial archives and supports systematic regional archaeological prioritization to be deployed within integrated archaeological workflows.

title: CREST functions as a molecular bridge between neuron-specific enhancers and epigenetic regulators in mature motor neurons
abstract: Abstract Motor neuron development requires precise transcriptional regulation mediated in part by BAF (BRG1/BRM-associated factor) chromatin remodeling complexes. The neuron-specific BAF subunit CREST is critical for neuronal function and is mutated in some cases of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), yet its underlying genomic mechanisms remain unclear. Using mouse embryonic stem cell differentiation, we show that CREST is essential for motor neuron maturation by activating mature neuronal genes and repressing progenitor genes. Mechanistically, CREST interacts with the neuronal transcription factors ONECUT1 and NGN2, and the BRM ATPase to target pre-existing accessible enhancers of neuronal genes. CREST deletion selectively prevents CBP histone acetyltransferase recruitment, reducing histone H3K27 acetylation at these enhancers and downregulating target gene expression, without disrupting BRM binding, enhancer accessibility, or long-range chromatin architecture. Overall, our findings identify CREST as a crucial epigenetic mediator bridging lineage-specific transcription factors, BAF complexes, and CBP to activate enhancers and promote proper motor neuron development.

title: Disability related disparities in diagnosis and survival of digestive system cancers in Northern Italy
abstract: Abstract Individuals with disabilities may experience disparities in cancer diagnosis, but population-based evidence remains limited. We conduct a population-based cohort study using linked cancer registry and administrative healthcare data for digestive system cancers diagnosed between 2018 and 2021 in Northern Italy, examining diagnostic routes and one-year survival according to pre-existing impairments. Individuals with impairments are more likely to be diagnosed following emergency presentation compared with those without impairments (51.8% compared with 37.9%; adjusted odds ratio 1.41, 95% confidence interval 1.23–1.61), particularly those with impairments of mental and neuromusculoskeletal functions. They also have higher one-year mortality (hazard ratio 1.36, 95% confidence interval 1.26–1.46), independent of socio-demographic and clinical factors. Here, we show that disability-related disparities in emergency cancer diagnosis and survival persist across multiple impairment categories, providing population-based evidence from a European setting on differences in diagnostic pathways across heterogeneous disability groups.

title: Transposable element-mediated structural variations shape gene expression and agronomic trait diversity in Brassica napus
Sex-specific intergenerational epigenetic responses to real-world chemical mixture exposure in an outbred sheep model
abstract: Abstract Establishing whether real-world environmental chemical (EC) exposure can induce heritable epigenetic modifications in large, outbred mammals is key to determining long-term developmental impacts of the human exposome. Using an established biosolids-treated pasture (BS) sheep model, we investigated whether gestational exposure to low-level mixtures of EC induced heritable changes in DNA methylation across three generations of sheep. Reduced-representation bisulfite sequencing of liver, blood, and sperm, combined with a structured, lineage-controlled breeding design, revealed widespread but lineage- and sex-specific differentially methylated loci (DML) in F1 offspring, with detectable alterations evident in F2 and F3 descendants. Although most DML were unique to individual sire lineages, or to a single generation, subsets of loci showed repeated involvement across generations and were associated with altered gene expression in F3 descendants. Sperm from F1 males exhibited reduced methylation at numerous loci and, together with seminal plasma, revealed differential expression of several microRNAs. These effects, however, showed limited persistence in F2 males, indicative of intergenerational rather than fully transgenerational persistence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that complex, low-level chemical exposures can elicit recurrent, sexually dimorphic epigenetic responses in outbred species, but underscore the challenge of disentangling exposure-induced inheritance from genetically regulated methylation variation.

title: Long-term nitrous acid evolution modulates ozone and secondary aerosol variations in global megacities
H3K27M cooperates with ASCL1 to maintain progenitor states and drive gliomagenesis
abstract: Abstract Histone 3 lysine 27-to-methionine substitutions (H3K27M) drive aggressive diffuse midline gliomas by blocking differentiation of radial glial progenitor cells committed to oligodendrogenesis. We establish prolonged differentiation as a powerful tool to uncover regulators of glioma cell states and demonstrate that the pioneer transcription factor (TF) ASCL1 is a key mediator of H3K27M-driven plasticity and tumorigenesis. H3K27M prevents Polycomb silencing of ASCL1 , co-opting this TF to maintain oligodendroglial progenitor states. Consistently, ASCL1 loss drastically impairs tumor formation in vivo. Mechanistically, ASCL1 synergizes with H3K27M to redistribute the chromatin remodeler BRG1 to regulatory elements co-enriched for ASCL1 and SOX motifs, promoting expression of stem and neural progenitor genes at the expense of mesenchymal genes in DMGs. ASCL1 loss acts as a “fire exit”, enabling alternative differentiation despite H3K27M, underscoring the therapeutic potential of targeting stalled differentiation and tumor plasticity in histone-mutant gliomas and cancers with a stem cell hierarchy.

title: Quantum-sensing-based super-resolution live cell microenvironment imaging
Structural basis of ammonium transport and coordinated regulation of AMT1;1 in Arabidopsis thaliana
abstract: Abstract Efficient ammonium uptake is essential for plant growth and nitrogen-use efficiency, yet the structural basis of ammonium transport and regulation in plant AMTs remains unclear. Here, we determined multiple cryo-electron microscopy structures of the Arabidopsis thaliana ammonium transporter AMT1;1 in apo, ammonium-bound, methylammonium-bound, low-pH and phosphomimetic states. These structures reveal a conserved ammonium conduction pathway comprising an aromatic recruitment vestibule, a Phe-gate/Twin-His-containing pore, and a polar intracellular exit region. We further identified a conserved extracellular N-terminal disulfide bond required for oligomer stability and transport activity, suggesting potential redox-dependent regulation. On the cytoplasmic side, phosphorylation modulates C-terminal interactions with intracellular loops, revealing an allosteric regulatory mechanism. Comparison with the bacterial ammonium-sensing protein Sd -Amt1 uncovers a conserved ammonium-recognition region in At AMT1;1 that contributes to transport activity but lacks the signaling module and ligand-dependent conformational switching observed in Sd -Amt1. Together, these findings provide structural insight into ammonium transport and coordinated regulation in plant AMT transporters.

title: Twisted superconducting quantum diodes for high fidelity anharmonic qubits
abstract: Abstract In superconducting circuits, bidirectional signal propagation can cause back-reflections and back-action that couple environmental noise back to coherent elements, degrading fidelity. Nonreciprocal superconducting diodes provide an intrinsic route to suppress such back-scattering at the circuit level. However, their diode efficiency and quantum integration remain limited. Here, we realize a quantum diode in twisted NbSe 2 under in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields. A mere 1 ∘ twist yields an efficiency enhancement over pristine devices, reaching 27.6%. Quantum simulations reveal that this intermediate efficiency, well below 100% ideal, is both experimentally practical and optimal for preserving qubit anharmonicity and stabilizing two-level systems. These findings show that maximal rectification is not always beneficial for quantum information, establishing a new principle for designing the fundamental properties of twisted superconductors towards low-power, high-fidelity quantum circuits.

title: Corpus Callosum Dysgenesis is concomitant with reduced metacognitive efficiency and sensitivity across multiple cohorts and modalities
Asymmetric bloom lengthening drives high-latitude ocean chlorophyll accumulation imbalance
Intrinsically flexible inorganic piezoelectric subnanowire enables wireless wearable bioelectronics for non-invasive multimodal human-machine interfacing
Somatosensory cortex shapes perceptual decision bias via the superior colliculus
abstract: Abstract Sensory inputs reach cortical and subcortical areas in parallel, but how they coordinate to guide decisions remains unknown. We examined the roles of the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the superior colliculus (SC) in mice performing whisker-mediated tactile detection. While inactivating S1 contralateral to the stimulus increased detection threshold, inactivating ipsilateral S1 decreased it. These opposing effects reflected shifts in choice bias rather than sensitivity. Unilateral SC inactivation produced similar directional effects, whereas bilateral inactivation of either S1 or SC neutralized bias. Furthermore, SC lesions impaired detection performance, and combined S1 inactivation caused no further impairment, indicating that S1-mediated shifts in bias were SC-dependent. S1 inactivation also decreased sensory-evoked neural activity in SC, and choice decoding revealed that behavioral impairment was more closely associated with changes in SC population activity than with loss of sensory encoding in S1. Thus, S1 shapes perceptual bias by modulating SC-dependent circuits that transform sensory evidence into perceptual decisions.

title: Governing global capital: How state capacity and climate policy credibility attract sustainable investment
abstract: Abstract Can governments steer global capital toward public goals in an era of market-driven finance? This paper examines how state capacity and institutional credibility enable governments to attract sustainable investment through climate policy. Using the adoption of climate policies across 94 economies, we apply a triple difference-in-differences design to distinguish the effects of policy announcements, implementation, and demonstrated performance. We find that announcements increase sustainable investment flows by 24 basis points per week even before policies take effect, while the effect rises to 45 basis points following implementation. Demonstrated policy performance further amplifies these flows: above-median improvements in emissions, renewable energy generation, and green innovation attract an additional 13–16 basis points per week. By contrast, improvements in financial returns and risk do not explain these flows. The study bridges the literature on state capacity and sustainable finance, showing that credible, high-capacity governance is foundational for mobilizing private capital toward climate goals—a critical insight for designing effective climate governance.

title: Extensive genomic diversity in Desulfovibrio reveals species-specific functional traits associated with disease
abstract: Abstract Desulfovibrio spp. are associated with inflammatory diseases and human health, yet limited representative genomes and isolates hinder our understanding of their role in disease. Here, we assembled a comprehensive database of 2658 Desulfovibrio genomes across 90 diseases and 32 countries, including 24 human isolates. Genomic analyses showed extensive species diversity and revealed disease-associated functional traits, including flagellin and adaptation-associated genes (i.e., ureases). Flagellin-mediated Toll-like receptor 5 activation was species-specific and D. desulfuricans flagellin downregulated TGF-beta signalling in murine small intestinal organoids, suggesting impaired immune tolerance. Additionally, we investigated genomic capacity for hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) production, a main Desulfovibrio metabolite. While health- and disease-associated Desulfovibrio spp. mainly encoded dissimilatory sulfate reduction, tetrathionate metabolism-encoding bacteria were exclusively detected in inflammatory bowel diseases, including Proteus mirabilis and Morganella morganii . Overall, our study provides a comprehensive genomic Desulfovibrio resource and identifies new links associating strain variation, functional traits and H 2 S-production with inflammatory diseases.

title: PRPF19 drives hepatic stellate cell activation and liver fibrosis via PKM2-mediated glycolytic reprogramming
A method quantifying soil melanin to understand fungal impacts on soil carbon stability
abstract: Abstract Fungal necromass, particularly dead microbial cells rich in melanin, is an important contributor to long-term soil carbon stabilization. Progress in understanding the role of soil melanin is limited by the lack of validated analytical methods. DNA-based approaches estimate only the genetic potential for melanin production and therefore provide indirect evidence of melanin occurrence. To directly assess soil melanin, we evaluated spectroscopic and spectrophotometric assays; however, both approaches proved insufficiently specific due to interference from chemically related compounds. Here, we introduce a liquid chromatography method that enables quantification of major fungal melanin types in soils. By enabling direct quantification of fungal melanin in soil, this framework allows longstanding hypotheses regarding melanized fungal necromass and soil carbon stabilization to be tested mechanistically. Here, we show with the proposed method that soil melanin concentrations are strongly correlated with total soil carbon, supporting a central role for fungal melanin in long-term soil carbon stabilization.

title: In situ reduction-driven formation of sub-nanometer alternating heterostructures
From revision to learning transfer: Self- and socially shared-regulated pathways in AI-assisted feedback
Designing a pipeline linking professional development to AI-driven instructional practices
Rethinking cultural awareness in think-aloud research
Disengaged Conversational Behaviors and Learning in Student-AI Dialogues for Mathematical Problem Solving
abstract: As the conversational AI agents become integrated into digital learning environments, students’ interaction with these systems can show conversational disengagement, including mocking, misleading, or otherwise diverting the agents. Although task-based disengagement such as gaming the system and off-task actions are well documented, the nature of the consequences of this conversational disengagement in student-AI dialogue remains largely unexplored. This study examined how different types of conversational disengagement relate to middle-school students’ mathematical learning with an AI-powered teachable agent embedded in a large-scale platform. We coded 5,522 utterances from 246 students into six conversational disengagement categories (False Answering, Mocking, Ghosting, Mirroring, Withholding, and Random/Noisy) versus engagement. Regression analyses showed that some disengagements (False Answering and Mocking) were positively associated with post-test scores after controlling for pre-test performance, although these associations did not replicate in a sensitivity analysis restricted to human-annotated utterances. To capture process-level dynamics, we modeled how conversational disengagement ends using a competing-risks approach and separately clustered students based on their turn-by-turn transition probabilities. Most conversational disengagement tended to end within the first few turns, whereas Withholding showed a strong tendency to continue. Students in the highest-performing cluster combined a moderate level of conversational disengagement with strong recovery pathways, whereas the lowest-performing cluster exhibited persistent self-loops without recovery. Together, these findings suggest that some apparent disengagement in conversation with AI may occur within interaction trajectories that subsequently return to productive engagement.

title: Efficient stabilizer or deadweight effect? The impact of subsidies for apprenticeship training during an economic downturn
